newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 26.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 26.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Changes to NZ First's plans for compulsory savings would lock hundreds of thousands of people into savings schemes without a guarantee that their money was safe. As coalition talks enter their final week, the party has issued an "explanation" of its saving policy that differs significantly from the policy it issued before the election. The new policy drops the promise of a government guarantee for people's compulsory savings. Page 1.

More jobs and better opportunities for exporters were the tangible benefits for New Zealand arising from the Apec meeting, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Monday night. Speaking from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' summit in the Philippines, Bolger said the individual action plans that Apec countries signed this year -- for achieving world trade liberalisation -- were "the beginning". Page 2.

Labour is seeking talks with the Alliance this week as a final step toward cementing Alliance support for a possible Labour-led coalition government. A spokesman for Labour leader Helen Clark said she was hoping to meet Alliance leader Jim Anderton later this week to discuss the Alliances "Issues Paper", a 20-page policy document outlining common policies between the Alliance, Labour and NZ First. Page 2.

Northern hemisphere fishing fleets would increasingly breach New Zealand's exclusive economic zone as fish stocks are wiped out in international waters, Fisheries Minister Doug Kidd said on Monday. He said the high seas were the nautical equivalent of a jungle, where fishing fleets operated with a "gold-rush mentality", cleaning out stocks before other fleets could do so. Page 2.

Policy modifications likely under either of the coalition government scenarios were unlikely to threaten the thrust of existing government policy, Moody's Investors Service said on Monday. In its annual report on New Zealand, the international ratings agency said New Zealand's economic fundamentals were solid and both main political parties were committed to the existing broad policy parameters. Page 3.

The biggest October quarter trade deficit on record confirmed concerns about an increasing current account shortfall and would tighten the focus on the exchange rate, economists said on Monday. Statistics NZ said on Monday that imports exceeded exports by $845 million during the quarter. This was the biggest deficit for an October quarter and the third biggest quarterly deficit on record. Economists said that though the quarter's figures were poor, they would not yet trigger a trade-deficit crisis. Page 15.

The Stock Exchange's TeNZ fund has some new competition with the arrival of three new passive investment funds, aiming to raise tens of millions of dollars. Sir Francis Renouf launched the Renouf New Zealand First Fifteen and Second Fifteen funds on Monday, holding shares in the top 15 listed companies and the next group of 15 respectively. Tower Trust Services recently set up the Tortis-New Zealand Fund, another index-linked investment fund. Page 15.

Qantas has forked out about $50 million to help Air New Zealand buy its stake in Ansett. The Australian national carrier said it now held 562.9 million B shares after Air NZ's renounceable rights issue, compared with the 420 million it owned previously. Page 15.
New Zealand Oil and Gas earned $3.2 million in cash operating profit in the first quarter of the current financial year, chairman Tony Radford said on Monday. Page 15.

DB Group said on Monday that it had $90 million to $95 million in surplus cash amd might announce a return of capital to shareholders when it issued full-year results next month. Since mid-October, the company's shares have risen about 20 percent amid talk of some type of capital return to shareholders. Page 16.

Bank of New Zealand will lose about seven percent of its loan portfolio when its Australian branch becomes part of parent National Australia Bank in mid-1997. The branch will be renamed Bank of New Zealand Australia. Page 16.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD
Children across the country are being recruited to dob in shops selling cigarettes to minors. Public health staff are asking volunteers aged around 13 to help test selected shops.

NZ First has denied modifying its compulsory superannuation policy, signalling that it will continue to take a tough line on the issue in the coalition talks. Labour and National were both bemused by the timing of the release at a sensitive stage in the coalition negotiations, in which NZ First detailed its plans for
super. The party's leader Winston Peters indicated that the release was designed to answer criticism last week from the Council of Trade Unions.

Good news for exporters and good news for jobs. That is how the Prime Minister summed up the impact of Apec on New Zealand during the forum's leaders' summit on Monday. Jim Bolger, who said he had talks with every Apec leader including United States President Bill Clinton, was upbeat about the summit and opportunities it offered for meeting leaders of major economies.

Foreign investors are not showing concern about the influence NZ First on the country's economic direction, according to company director Rosanne Meo. Meo, a director of Ports of Auckland and Mercury Energy, was a New Zealand representative at the business advisory council meeting of Apec in Manila.

Labour is relaxed about comments made by one of its key negotiators Mike Moore, warning NZ First leader Winston Peters that his supporters will feel a sense of betrayal if NZ First does a deal with National. A spokesman for Labour leader Helen

Clark said Moore was simply expressing what the polls were saying. A National Business Review-Consultus poll on Friday found that 62 percent of NZ First supporters wanted a link with Labour. Just 22 percent favoured a deal with National.

Qantas is believed to have begun moves to sell its 19.4 percent stake in Air New Zealand. United States institutions have been offered a large block of stock in Air NZ, which is thought to be that of the Australian carrier. The possible exit of Qantas comes at a time when Air NZ is looking to forge strategic alliances with other international airlines. It is

understood that a group of Air NZ management is in the United States talking to United Airlines. This could lead to a code sharing agreement between the two airlines, which would broaden Air NZ's service between North America and Europe.

Potential raiders of New Zealand Oil and Gas were warned "to keep their hands off" by the chairman Tony Radford at the annual meeting in Auckland on Monday. Earlier this month, NZOG spent $1.5 million to buy 3.2 million shares to head off such a group, some of whom Radford said he believed had since sold out. This defensive action had potentially saved a lot of executive time
and money, he said.

Only a handful of the 250 New Zealand members of Lloyd's of London risk being sued under the insurance market's "Reconstruction and Renewal" plan. Newly appointed Lloyd's chief executive Ron Sandler said in Auckland on Monday that the plan had received 97 percent acceptance from New Zealand members.
